overview:
Organisation of Science and Technology K–6

Figure 1 shows the organisation of Science and Technology K–6, highlighting the common practices of science, design and digital technologies. The organisation of interrelated practices across content reflects the role of these practices in developing scientific, design and technological knowledge. Across a stage of learning all focus areas need to be taught.

Image long description: The diagram has 2 columns headed Science and Technologies. Listed under the heading Science are the 4 focus areas: Observations and questions spark curiosity; Investigations of changes provide knowledge and understanding; Physical and living systems depend on energy; and Knowledge of our world and beyond inspires sustainable solutions. The 4 focus areas for Technologies are: Observations and questions initiate design and digital solutions; Design and digital solutions are created through knowledge and understanding; Design processes and digital systems are used to create solutions; and Design and digital technologies engineer sustainable solutions. Both subject areas are circled by a line labelled Applying knowledge, understanding and skills through interrelated practices.

Protocols for collaborating with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Communities

NESA is committed to working in partnership with Aboriginal Communities and supporting teachers, schools and schooling sectors to improve educational outcomes for young people.

It is important to respect appropriate ways of interacting with Aboriginal Communities and Cultural material when teachers plan, program and implement Science and Technology learning experiences that focus on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities.

Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) protocols need to be followed. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ ICIP protocols include Cultural Knowledges, Cultural Expression and Cultural Property and documentation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ Identities and lived experiences. It is important to recognise the diversity and complexity of different Cultural groups in NSW, as protocols may differ between local Aboriginal Communities.

Teachers should work in partnership with Elders, parents, Community members, Cultural Knowledge Holders, or a local, regional or state Aboriginal Education Consultative Group. It is important that respect for Elders and for the roles of men and women is shown. Local Aboriginal Peoples should be invited to share their Cultural Knowledges with students and staff when engaging with Aboriginal histories and Cultural Practices.

Creating written texts supports learning

The Science and Technology K–6 Syllabus follows Recommendation 2: ‘Clarify and strengthen writing content in syllabus documents’ from Teaching Writing: Report of the Thematic Review of Writing (NESA 2018).

Creating written texts is a way of organising thoughts, explaining thinking, and making connections within and across learning areas. The learning areas provide meaningful content for writing beyond the subject of English. ‘When writing instruction prompts students to think deeply and/or make decisions about content, learning is improved’ (AERO 2022). Creating written texts in learning areas develops students’ critical understandings and voice.

Creating written texts content in the primary curriculum includes:

  • systematic development of expectations for creating written texts, which aligns with the English K–10 Syllabus (2022)
  • explicit writing content to support students to become fluent creators of texts, to deepen their understanding of the learning areas
  • opportunities to practise the process of creating written texts to develop and communicate knowledge, understanding and ideas
  • a focus on vocabulary and sentence construction.

Creating written texts refers to the act of composing and constructing a text for a particular purpose, audience and context.

Various methods of transcription may be employed, and a student’s preferred communication form(s) should be considered when teaching writing.

overviewSections.heading: Access content points
overviewSections.html:
Access content points have been developed to support students with significant intellectual disability who are working towards Early Stage 1 outcomes. These students may communicate using verbal and/or nonverbal forms.

For each of the Early Stage 1 outcomes, access content points are provided to indicate content that students with significant intellectual disability may access as they work towards the outcomes. Teachers will use the access content points on their own, or in combination with the content for each outcome. 

Decisions regarding curriculum options for students with disability should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning.

overviewSections.heading: The importance of knowledge and vocabulary in the primary curriculum
overviewSections.html:
The attainment of knowledge is a key goal of education. There is accumulated knowledge and wisdom of our world that all students have a right to learn. The curriculum plays a key role in identifying shared knowledge that provides opportunities to foster belonging and cross-cultural understanding in our society.

Knowledge underpins our ability to think and do. Students learn new ideas with reference to their existing knowledge. In each learning area, background knowledge committed to long-term memory is vital to literacy development and underpins the ability to think critically and creatively.

When learning to read, it is the development of broad knowledge, alongside vocabulary, which supports students to build mental models from the texts they engage with, secure schemas of increasing depth and complexity, and make connections with their world. Learning opportunities within the primary curriculum are coherent, intentional and designed to build knowledge and vocabulary of the learning area and support literacy development.

rationale:
The study of Science and Technology in K–6 fosters a student’s sense of wonder about the world around them and knowledge of how it works. Scientific and technological knowledge is revised, refined and advanced as new evidence arises. Learning about science and technology provides a framework for students to know, understand and make sense of the world. This study encourages students to embrace new concepts and learn to observe, develop testable questions, and test and evaluate ideas to refine their understanding.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples have used scientific and technological methods to understand and make connections with and between People and their land, sea and sky for tens of thousands of years. Linking traditional and contemporary knowledge enables students to make meaningful connections with everyday lives and develop cultural competence.

Understanding the abundant and increasingly accessible information in the world is foundational to becoming informed and active citizens. In responding to dynamic environments, students are required to understand and evaluate ever-increasing amounts of information gathered from varied sources. Students are provided with opportunities to develop technological literacy skills through the use of digital technologies and the design and production of creative solutions.

The syllabus intends to build on students’ natural curiosity and inventiveness, providing opportunities to explore the natural and designed world, test ideas, and make decisions based on data and evidence.
aim:
The aim of the Science and Technology K–6 Syllabus is for students to develop:

  • scientific and technological knowledge, skills, practices and dispositions
  • an understanding of natural phenomena and ways in which science and technologies can be used for the benefit of humanity and the planet
  • an understanding, through application, of the processes that can be used to create solutions or products that benefit society
  • an interest to further their knowledge in science, technology and engineering
  • the ability to participate in society as scientifically and technologically literate, engaged citizens.

focusAreas.title: Observations and questions initiate design and digital solutions

outcomes.description: identifies and uses technologies to make products to address user needs or opportunities
poses questions based on observations to collect data

contentGroups.title: Understanding user needs inspires design and digital solutions

items.text: Distinguish between user needs and wants and describe how they can lead to design opportunities
Identify designed products and how they meet user needs
items.examples: Packaging of food products, wheelchairs, motion sensor doors.

items.text: Design and build a simple product that addresses a user need or opportunity
items.examples: A bridge that supports the weight of a toy, a shelter for an animal, a bag for carrying stationery.

items.text: Pose questions to identify the parts of plants and animals used for food and fibre and create a data display
items.examples: Image long description: Six-column data display with labels and examples: Root – carrot, Stem – celery, Leaf – lettuce, Flower – cauliflower, Fruit – apple, Seed – peas.

items.text: Examine designed structures that animals build to help them survive in their environment
items.examples: Ant nests, beehives, bowerbird nests, spider webs.

items.text: Identify and safely use digital devices and apps for a purpose
items.examples: Take a photograph, audio recording or videorecording of people or objects, with permission, to share with others. Use digital input devices such as a keyboard, microphone, mouse or stylus to label pictures or to operate a search engine to identify an animal or plant.

items.text: Follow a series of steps to record, save and retrieve data
items.examples: Take a photo on a device. Open it in an app. Label it and save it.

outcomes.description: identifies and describes characteristics of living things, properties of materials, and movement
poses questions based on observations to collect data

contentGroups.title: Living things have characteristics that help them survive in their environment

items.text: Identify the sense organs and describe their functions
Identify and use tools to aid and extend sensory observations
items.examples: Bug jars or boxes for insects or earthworms; magnifying glass; digital photography; hearing aids.

items.text: Describe how living things get air, water and energy to survive in their environment
Recognise that plants produce their own food, and animals need to find their food
Examine flowers, fruit, leaves, roots and stems of plants and describe their purpose
items.examples: Roots take in water; stems carry water to the leaves which take in sunlight as energy.

items.text: Examine animal bodies, their body coverings, and how and what they eat
items.examples: Image long description: A photo of a sulphur-crested cockatoo with the following features labelled: a strong beak to break seeds, wings, feathers to help it fly, and claws to hold objects.

items.text: Observe and group animals based on their characteristics and justify the grouping
Describe ways Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples use Knowledges of the characteristics of plants and animals to survive
items.examples: A Banksia flower can be used as a source of food, the cone as a water purifier and as a torch.

items.text: Pose questions to compare the characteristics of living things and non-living things
items.examples: What makes a thing living? Living things have needs, reproduce and a life span.

contentGroups.title: Objects are made of materials that have observable properties

items.text: Recognise that properties of materials can be observed using the senses
items.examples: Colour, size, shape, texture, warmth, sound, scent.

items.text: Observe and manipulate materials to describe their properties using Tier 2 vocabulary
items.examples: Observe with a magnifying glass, rub together. Hard, flexible, smooth, transparent, warm, squeaky.

items.text: Pose questions about materials and describe how they are used in everyday objects
items.examples: Why do helmets need to be hard? Why are plates sometimes made of paper, plastic, bamboo, ceramics or food?

items.text: Bend, twist, crush and stretch objects to show that the properties of materials remain the same
items.examples: Crushed chalk, knitted wool, origami.

items.text: Explore how Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples use natural materials for specific purposes based on their properties
items.examples:
Art: painting techniques, ochre, weaving.

Tools: Grinding stones, boomerang.

contentGroups.title: Living things and objects move in different ways

items.text: Observe, describe and categorise the ways in which living things move
items.examples: Crawling, flying, swimming.

items.text: Identify and label the parts of the human body that are used for movement
items.examples:
Bones: elbow, knee, knuckles, spine.

Muscles: calf, thigh.

items.text: Test how the movement of an object is affected by its shape
items.examples:
Movement: bounce, roll, slide.

Direction: straight line, zigzag, veering to one side.

Objects: ball, box, cone, cylinder, egg.

items.text: Experiment to observe how an object’s movement is affected by its material
items.examples: Cloth, metal, plastic, rubber, wood, wool.

items.text: Identify objects made by Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples and describe their movements
items.examples: Boomerang, woomera, grinding stone, axe, digging stick, canoe.

contentGroups.title: Creating written sentences supports understanding of Science and Technology

items.text: Select adjectives to add precision when describing the properties of materials
items.examples: Elastic, fragile, rigid, opaque.

items.text: Use nouns, adjectives and verbs to label pictures to describe the characteristics or movement of living things
Use subject–verb–object structure to create simple sentences to describe how living things meet their needs

focusAreas.title: Investigations of changes provide knowledge and understanding

outcomes.description: measures and describes changes in living things, materials, movement, Earth and the sky
poses questions based on observations and information to investigate cause and effect
collects, represents and uses data to identify patterns and relationships

contentGroups.title: Living things change over time

items.text: Recognise that data can be collected through observation, testing and research, and that it can be represented as descriptions, diagrams, graphs, images and tables
Collect data about the variety of living things in a local habitat, group them and justify the groupings
Describe the changes in a plant as it grows using data and scientific models
items.examples:
Changes: seed, germination, roots grow down, stems grow up, leaves develop, plant gets larger, flowers may form, then fruit forms and ripens. Fruit contains seeds.

Scientific models: flow charts, labelled pictures.

items.text: Describe the changes in an animal as it goes through its life cycle using data and scientific models
items.examples: From silkworm to silk moth. Scientific models: 3D models, algorithms, labelled pictures, flow charts.

items.text: Describe how Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples use Knowledges of the life cycles of livings things
items.examples: Bogong moth, grass trees (Xanthorrhoea spp.)

items.text: Examine the evidence for extinct animals
items.examples: Fossils, models of dinosaurs. Australian megafauna: Thylacoleo, Diprotodon. Images of Thylacine.

contentGroups.title: Light and sound interact with materials in different ways

items.text: Recognise that light and sound can travel through air, water and some solids and are affected by those materials
Pose questions, test and describe how light can be reflected, refracted, dispersed or absorbed by materials
items.examples: A mirror reflects light. A pencil in a glass of water to see the effect of refraction. A prism disperses light, forming a rainbow. Cardboard absorbs light.

items.text: Describe how translucent, transparent, opaque and reflective materials interact with light
items.examples: Cellophane, a window, a wall, a mirror.

items.text: Recognise that sound is created and carried by vibrations
Observe how Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples use a range of materials and actions to create sound for specific purposes
items.examples: Emu caller is used for collecting emu eggs, percussion (e.g. clapsticks) and wind instruments are used in song and dance.

items.text: Test how different materials and actions affect the volume and pitch of sound
items.examples:
Materials: plastic, metal, wood.

Actions: blow, pluck, scrape, shake, strike.

contentGroups.title: The human body’s sense organs detect its environment

items.text: Recognise that the human brain detects information about the surroundings using sense organs, and that it controls and coordinates body functions
Observe and describe the function and parts of the eye and the ear
items.examples:
Eye: iris, pupil, lens, eyelid, eyelashes, tears.

Ear: external ear, ear lobe, eardrum.

items.text: Investigate how taste and smell provide information about the environment
items.examples: Taste can indicate dangerous foods and provide comfort and enjoyment. Smell can indicate danger, help source food and help make inferences about the environment.

items.text: Pose questions, test and describe textures to investigate the sense of touch
items.examples: Rough, hairy, spongy, jagged, coarse, crumbly, sharp.

contentGroups.title: Forces can change the way objects move

items.text: Recognise that a force is a push or a pull that can make things either start moving, stop moving, change speed, direction or shape
Pose questions and test the effects of forces on an object's movement
items.examples: Playground equipment, toys, windows, doors, kitchen equipment.

items.text: Investigate how applied forces change the movement of traditional toys and tools used by Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples
items.examples: Propeller toys, spinning tops.

items.text: Test how frictional forces affect moving objects
items.examples: Carpet, plastic, rubber, timber.

items.text: Test how the force of magnetism affects objects
items.examples: Attraction and repulsion between magnets. Test materials to determine whether they are magnetic.

contentGroups.title: Planet Earth is our home

items.text: Observe and record daily weather to identify changes and patterns
items.examples: Cloud cover, rainfall, temperature.

items.text: Investigate how seasonal patterns influence the behaviour and appearance of living things
items.examples: Seasonal flowers, deciduous trees, hibernation, migration.

items.text: Describe the ways in which Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples use seasonal indicators
items.examples: Indications for times for planting, harvesting, breeding seasons, Cultural burning.

items.text: Observe and identify rocks in natural formations and those used in built structures
items.examples: Granite, marble, sandstone, slate. Beaches, buildings, statues, road cuttings.

items.text: Manipulate different rocks and describe their texture, colour and grain or crystal size

contentGroups.title: The sky is our window to the Universe

items.text: Describe the visible features of the sky at night and in the day
items.examples:
Night: stars, Moon, Milky Way.

Day: Sun, clouds, occasionally the Moon.

items.text: Recognise that the Sun provides Earth with light energy and the Moon reflects light energy from the Sun
Recognise that the Sun rises in the east and sets in the west
Model how the rotation of the Earth around its axis causes a repeating pattern of day and night
Record changes in shadow length at different times of the day to mark the passage of time
items.examples: Minimal shadows at noon, long shadows in the early morning or late afternoon.

items.text: Observe the Moon over a lunar cycle and describe its change in appearance using Tier 2 and Tier 3 vocabulary
items.examples: Crescent, full, gibbous, half, new, waning, waxing.

items.text: Describe Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ connections to Sky Country
items.examples: Dreaming Stories of the Seven Sisters, Emu in the sky; navigation and wayfinding.

items.text: Examine cultural representations of the Sun, Moon and stars
items.examples: Flags, ancient Roman, Greek, Egyptian and Chinese stories; art and music.

contentGroups.title: Creating written texts supports understanding of Science and Technology

items.text: Use nouns, noun groups and verbs to create notes, annotations and labels to document observations
Use simple and compound sentences, flow charts and labelled diagrams to describe a process or function
items.examples: Use multimodal texts to describe the life cycle of a plant or animal, the effects of forces on an object’s movement, the function and parts of the human eye.

items.text: Sequence simple and compound sentences, and use labelled diagrams and data to describe cause and effect

focusAreas.title: Design and digital solutions are created through knowledge and understanding

outcomes.description: uses technologies and materials to design and make products to address user needs or opportunities
poses questions based on observations and information to investigate cause and effect

contentGroups.title: A design process is used to define user needs and create solutions

items.text: Recognise that a design process breaks large projects into manageable, logical steps
items.examples: Define, research, generate ideas, plan, make, test, evaluate. An iterative process.

items.text: Pose questions and test how materials with different properties contribute to the effectiveness of a product
items.examples: What are the best materials to use to make maracas? What would happen if the material from which an object was made was changed?

items.text: Apply one or more steps of a design process to make a product
Describe how food and fibre can be designed and produced to address user needs
items.examples: Olives for oil, cotton plant for fabric, sustainable timber for building.

items.text: Describe the ways in which Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples design using natural materials for specific purposes
items.examples: Using kangaroo sinew as rope when making tools or plant fibres for sewing animal furs and weaving.

items.text: Describe how products, including digital systems, can affect people’s lives
items.examples:
Products: book, dishwasher, prosthetic.

Digital systems: barcode scanner, audiobook, augmentative and alternative communication (AAC), contactless payments.

contentGroups.title: Digital systems use inputs and algorithms to produce an output

items.text: Describe how digital systems are used in everyday life and for learning
items.examples: Access to digital medical services for regional and remote communities, Aboriginal Language apps, assistive technologies.

items.text: Identify digital systems that can be used to collect personal data and how to protect personal information
items.examples: Forms, cameras at the supermarket, CCTV, apps. Security of usernames and passwords or passphrases.

items.text: Create a sequential algorithm that controls a digital device
items.examples: Program a sprite to move across a screen. Program directions for a friend or a bot to follow, using half-turn, left and right instructions.

items.text: Use the basic features of common digital tools to capture, save and retrieve data to communicate and collaborate following agreed rules
items.examples:
Tools: image software, video recording.

Rules: keeping passwords and personal information, including photos and videos, private. Assertively gain, give or deny consent to share information.

focusAreas.title: Design processes and digital systems are used to create solutions

outcomes.description: uses a design process to create products to address user needs or opportunities
designs and uses algorithms, represents data and uses digital systems for a purpose

contentGroups.title: Design is a process of creating and innovating

items.text: Explore the design of a structure, product or place and identify how user needs are addressed
items.examples: Space station, search engine, learning area, accessible playground, sensory space.

items.text: Generate, develop and communicate design ideas
items.examples: Thumbnail sketches, models, annotated drawings, materials required. Represent algorithms as a list of steps or a diagram.

items.text: Test construction methods and materials to build a designed model
Build, test and evaluate a designed model
Research processes used to provide food and clothing
items.examples: Technologies to support growth, harvest, preservation, transport and sale.

contentGroups.title: Digital systems can be created and controlled

items.text: Use core features of common digital tools to locate, select, store and retrieve relevant information
items.examples: Refine search terms, bookmark relevant sources.

items.text: Use core features of common digital tools to share content, plan tasks and collaborate safely following an agreed code of conduct
items.examples: Assertively gain, give or deny consent to share information online, keep personal information safe.

items.text: Design algorithms that use branching and iteration to document and program a procedure
Explore how data can be represented by letters, numbers, symbols, images and sounds depending on the purpose
items.examples: Charts, graphs, Morse code, music notation, semaphore.

items.text: Select, enter and represent different types of data using digital tools
items.examples:
Types of data: text, image, audio, video.

Tools: image software, spreadsheets, word processors.

focusAreas.title: Physical and living systems depend on energy

outcomes.description: uses information to investigate the solar system and the effects of energy on living, physical and geological systems
poses questions to create fair tests that investigate the effects of energy on living things and physical systems
uses and interprets data to describe patterns and relationships

contentGroups.title: Living things depend on energy and materials to survive

items.text: Identify the systems of Earth that make up environments: air – atmosphere, land – lithosphere, water – hydrosphere, living things – biosphere
Describe how the needs of living things are provided by the atmosphere, hydrosphere and lithosphere
items.examples:
Atmosphere: air and gases – oxygen.

Hydrosphere: water, aquatic habitats.

Lithosphere: nutrient-rich soil necessary for plant growth, terrestrial habitats.

items.text: Describe the relationship between habitat, ecosystem and environment
items.examples: Image long description: The innermost circle is labelled Habitat. It is surrounded by a second circle labelled Ecosystem, and an outer circle labelled Environment.

items.text: Observe and describe living and non-living things in a habitat
items.examples:
Living things: plants, animals, fungi, lichen.

Non-living things: type of soil, water.

items.text: Pose questions to conduct fair tests to determine the effects of soil, water and light energy on plants
items.examples: Gravel, mud, sand, soil; fresh or salt water; amount, colour, direction of light.

items.text: Describe how Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ practices support habitats to survive
items.examples: Cultural burning.

items.text: Describe the transfer of energy between plants and animals using food chains, Tier 2 and Tier 3 vocabulary
items.examples: Tree sap → cicada → lizard → kookaburra. Carnivore, consumer, decomposer, herbivore, omnivore, parasite, predator, prey, producer.

items.text: Describe ways in which plants and animals depend on each other for survival
items.examples:
Plants depend on animals: insect pollination of flowers, seed dispersal inside or outside animals.

Animals depend on plants: food, clothing and shelter.

contentGroups.title: Energy is required to change the properties of matter

items.text: Recognise that matter is anything that has mass, takes up space and consists of very small particles

Observe examples of matter that exist as a solid, which has a defined shape and volume; a liquid, which has a definite volume but not a definite shape; and a gas, which has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume
items.examples: At room temperature, solids: wood, plastic, rocks; liquids: milk, honey, water; gases: air, helium, natural gas.

items.text: Observe and describe water changing from solid to liquid to gas and back again, using Tier 2 and Tier 3 vocabulary
items.examples: Boiling, condensation, evaporation, freezing, melting.

items.text: Describe how adding and removing heat energy affects the movement and arrangement of particles when matter is changing state
items.examples:
‘States of matter’ by Yelod is licensed under CC BY-SA 3.0. The image has been adapted for this syllabus.
Image long description: Three cylinders represent a solid, a liquid and a gas. The solid cylinder contains small spheres packed together at the bottom of the cylinder in a defined shape. The cylinder for liquid contains small spheres in pairs that drift together at the bottom of the cylinder. The cylinder for gas contains small spheres that float randomly in pairs.

contentGroups.title: Body systems work together to enable movement

items.text: Recognise that all animals are either invertebrates with no spine, or vertebrates with a spine
items.examples:
Invertebrates with no spine or internal skeleton: earthworms, jellyfish, snails.

Invertebrates with no spine and an external skeleton: bees, crabs, spiders.

Vertebrates: birds, humans, sharks.

items.text: Compare ways invertebrates and vertebrates move on land, in water and in the sky
Recognise that the human muscular and skeletal systems work together to enable movement
Identify parts of the human skeleton that offer protection and support
items.examples:
Protection: skull, ribcage.

Support: spine, clavicle, pelvis.

items.text: Model how bones, muscles and joints work together to cause movement
items.examples: Hinge joint in knees and elbows; ball-and-socket joint in shoulders and hips. Specific names of bones and muscles are not required.

contentGroups.title: Heat energy can be transferred

items.text: Recognise that heat energy can be transferred from warmer to cooler objects by conduction, convection and radiation
Recognise that temperature is a measure of hotness or coldness, measured using a thermometer and often expressed in degrees Celsius
Pose questions and conduct fair tests to compare how different materials absorb or reflect heat energy
items.examples: Black materials vs white materials. Metals vs fabrics. Use a temperature sensor, probe, thermometer, ice.

items.text: Describe how the properties of materials and transfer of heat energy impact everyday life
items.examples: Clothing, insulation, shade.

contentGroups.title: Forces shape Earth’s surface

items.text: Investigate Aboriginal Dreaming Stories and Torres Strait Islander Legends about the formation of landscapes and landforms
items.examples: Jenolan Caves, Nobby’s Headland, Rainbow Serpent, Three Sisters (Gulu-mada).

items.text: Explain how the forces produced by wind, water and living things weather rocks
items.examples: Wind and water carry particles that hit against rocks. Plant roots grow into crevices in rocks.

items.text: Research and describe the changes to the landscape caused by earthquakes and volcanoes
Research, describe and model the internal structure of Earth
items.examples: Crust, mantle, outer and inner core; 2D diagrams, cutaway diagrams, 3D models.

items.text: Describe and model how forces produced by moving water cause erosion
items.examples: The faster the water moves, the greater the force exerted, which can move heavier objects.

contentGroups.title: The Sun is the centre of our solar system and provides our world with energy

items.text: Model Earth’s revolution around the Sun and recognise that a complete revolution takes 365.25 days
Research how energy from the Sun is used
items.examples: Drying clothes, solar cells, salt farms, sundried fruit, pizza box solar oven.

items.text: Describe features of our solar system using multimodal representations
items.examples: Features: size and composition of planets, moons, asteroids; relative length of day and year on each planet.

items.text: Demonstrate that gravity is a force of attraction between objects and Earth
items.examples: Drop an object from a height.

items.text: Recognise that the force of gravity keeps Earth, moons and planets in their positions in the solar system
Research cultural references to the solar system including Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Knowledges of the night sky
items.examples: Roman and Greek names of planets and days of the week, music and art, ancient Aztec and Inca astronomical observatories, Dreaming Stories, Torres Strait Islander Legends.

contentGroups.title: Creating written explanations of physical and living systems supports understanding of Science and Technology

items.text: Use Tier 2 and Tier 3 vocabulary and noun groups to enhance the specificity of texts
items.examples:
Vocabulary: asteroid, insulator, mantle.

Noun groups: heat energy, light source, seed dispersal.

items.text: Use notes, diagrams, flow charts and annotations to support understanding and explain processes
Use compound and complex sentences to sequence connected ideas into paragraphs when explaining cause and effect
items.examples: Changes caused by erosion, earthquakes or volcanoes and their effects on the landscape; interactions of Earth’s systems.

items.text: Use temporal and causal connectives and labelled diagrams when explaining the process of conducting a fair test
items.examples:
Temporal connectives: first, next, finally.

Causal connectives: because, due to, as a result.

focusAreas.title: Creating written texts in Science and Technology

outcomes.description: creates written texts to communicate understanding of scientific and technological concepts and processes

contentGroups.title: Creating written explanations of concepts and processes supports understanding of Science and Technology

items.text: Use nominalisations to convey scientific and technological concepts and processes succinctly
items.examples: Adaptation, innovation, insulation.

items.text: Add authority to written texts by using data to support an evidence-based explanation or argument
Use compound and complex sentences and labelled diagrams to create a text that explains a process, concept or investigation
items.examples: A causal explanation showing how the loss or introduction of a plant or animal has affected an Australian ecosystem; a plan for implementing a sustainable practice; a factual recount documenting the process of constructing and testing an electrical circuit.

items.text: Use notetaking, journalling, annotations and labelled images to create a multimodal text that documents the design processes involved in developing a solution
Acknowledge sources of information used in own texts

focusAreas.title: Design and digital technologies engineer sustainable solutions

outcomes.description: uses design processes to create, evaluate and modify designed solutions
creates, evaluates and modifies algorithms to code or control digital devices and systems

contentGroups.title: Design processes explore opportunities and develop solutions

items.text: Research Australian technologies and inventions that meet an identified need
items.examples: Mechanical sheep shears, cochlear implant, plastic skin, penicillin, wi-fi technology, polymer bank notes, permaculture.

items.text: Research how contemporary spaces are co-designed using Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Knowledge systems and Cultural Practices
items.examples: Bush food garden in a school, yarning circle spaces in a school playground.

items.text: Collect data about a user need to generate design criteria for sustainable solutions
items.examples: Surveys. Availability of materials, cost, sustainability of materials.

items.text: Develop design ideas to build a prototype using design criteria
Test, evaluate and modify the prototype to meet the design criteria

contentGroups.title: The future can be shaped by building and connecting digital systems

items.text: Recognise that data are entered, processed and transmitted in digital systems
items.examples:
Entering data: keystrokes, light, motion, sound.

Processing data: central processing unit (CPU), memory.

Transmitting data: wires, wi-fi.

items.text: Explore how and why data can be represented as binary code and in other forms
items.examples: Bar code, QR code. Zeros and ones indicate on and off states.

items.text: Create, test and modify algorithms as visual programs that include branching and iteration
items.examples:
Plugged: use a microprocessor, robot, screen-based product.

Unplugged: use flow charts, pseudocode, diagrams.

Physical coding: ‘paper, scissors, rock’ hand game; treasure map.

items.text: Select and use appropriate digital tools to share files online following an agreed code of conduct
items.examples:
Tools: Email, online document collaboration service.

Files: audio, image, video, word document.

Assertively gain, give or deny consent to share information online.

items.text: Evaluate a digital system that accepts and displays information
items.examples: Interface of a game or app. Evaluate ease of use, aesthetics, accessibility, appropriateness for intended audience.

items.text: Connect components in a digital system to collect data
items.examples: Plugged: collect environmental data by connecting sensors to microprocessors.

items.text: Use collected data to create an algorithm to perform a function
items.examples: Use data from moisture sensor to water plants: when soil moisture is below a nominated level, water plants; stop watering when soil moisture reaches a nominated level.

focusAreas.title: Knowledge of our world and beyond inspires sustainable solutions

outcomes.description: uses evidence to explain how scientific knowledge can be used to develop sustainable practices
poses questions to identify variables and conducts fair tests to gather data
interprets data to support explanations and arguments

contentGroups.title: Living things may change over millions of years, in response to their environments

items.text: Observe behavioural and structural adaptations of plants and animals, and suggest how these may help them survive in their environments
items.examples:
Behavioural adaptations: flowers close at night, burrowing or nocturnal behaviour in animals.

Structural adaptations: Banksias’ hard seed pods need fire to germinate, a thorny devil’s skin has ridges to channel water to its mouth.

items.text: Examine and explain how the characteristics of flowers, fruit and seeds are adaptations for reproduction in plants
items.examples:
Flowers: colour, scent and markings encourage pollination by birds or bees.

Fruit: source of sugar encourages animals to eat and disperse seeds.

Seeds: dispersal by wind, attachment to animals or being eaten by animals.

items.text: Interpret a food web that describes the flow of matter and energy between plants and animals in an ecosystem
Identify and describe how the loss or introduction of plants or animals affects an Australian ecosystem
items.examples:
Introduction: cane toad, prickly pear, rabbits, deer.

Loss: coral animals, mangroves.

items.text: Examine evidence that environments have changed over time and continue to change
items.examples: Fossil trees (Glossopteris) in Antarctica are evidence of changing climate. Cradle Mountain, Warrumbungles.

items.text: Describe how Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ sustainable practices continue to protect the environment
items.examples: Sharing environmental knowledge about how best to care for Country and Place, Totemic systems.

contentGroups.title: A fixed amount of usable matter makes up all the material on Earth

items.text: Explain how recyclable, reusable, renewable, biodegradable and compostable materials enhance sustainability
Recognise that in a fair test, an independent variable is changed, a dependent variable is measured, and controlled variables remain the same
Pose questions to determine whether substances dissolve in water by identifying variables and conducting and evaluating fair tests
items.examples:
Independent variable: substance (food colouring, oil, salt, sand, soil, sugar).

Dependent variable: time taken to dissolve.

Controlled variables: amount of substance, amount of water, stirring, temperature.

items.text: Investigate ways to collect and process waste to reduce pollution or increase the sustainable use of materials
items.examples: Batteries, electronic waste, food organics and garden organics, paper, plastics. Removal of pollution in waterways, sustainable packaging.

items.text: Create and communicate a plan to implement a sustainable practice in a community that addresses an identified environmental concern
items.examples: Management of a water environment, reduction of pollution.

contentGroups.title: Body systems coordinate for survival

items.text: Identify the main organs and their functions in the human digestive, respiratory and circulatory systems
items.examples:
Digestive: oesophagus, stomach, intestines break down and absorb nutrients.

Respiratory: trachea, bronchi, lungs take in oxygen from the air.

Circulatory: heart, arteries, veins pump blood around the body.

items.text: Recognise that the human digestive, respiratory and circulatory systems work together
Identify variables and conduct fair tests to describe ways the circulatory and respiratory systems respond to physical activity
items.examples:
Independent variable: physical activity.

Dependent variable: pulse rate.

Controlled variables: method and times of pulse taking, type of activity.

items.text: Investigate how structural and behavioural adaptations in humans aid survival
items.examples:
Structural adaptations: teeth and a varied diet, opposable thumbs, bipedalism.

Behavioural adaptations: long-term care and education of young.

contentGroups.title: Electrical energy can be transferred and transformed

items.text: Recognise that an electrical circuit transfers electrical energy from a source, through a pathway, to a device that transforms electrical energy into other forms of energy
items.examples:
Energy source: battery, mains socket.

Energy pathway: wire, printed circuit.

Device: light bulb, buzzer, fan.

items.text: Plan and construct simple electrical circuits to model the transfer and transformation of energy
items.examples: Use batteries, light bulbs, switches and insulated wires to set up a circuit. Diagrams, role-play, video.

items.text: Pose questions, identify variables and safely conduct fair tests to identify materials that act as electrical conductors or insulators
items.examples: Conductors such as metals; insulators such as rubber, wood.

items.text: Explain how electrical insulators can ensure electrical safety in everyday life
Identify renewable and non-renewable energy sources
items.examples:
Renewable: hydropower, solar power, tidal power and wind power.

Non-renewable: coal, nuclear power.

items.text: Research and present information describing the impact on resources and the environment of using a renewable or a non-renewable resource to generate electricity

contentGroups.title: Earth's climate is affected by natural and human activities

items.text: Identify the technologies used to collect weather data and describe how they are used
items.examples: Satellites, weather stations.

items.text: Describe the differences between climate and weather
Research the effects of natural events on the atmosphere
items.examples: Bushfires, ocean currents, volcanic eruptions.

items.text: Explain the effects of natural events and human activities on climate

contentGroups.title: Our solar system is a part of one of billions of galaxies in the Universe

items.text: Recognise stars, galaxies, nebulae, exoplanets and black holes as astronomical features that exist beyond our solar system
Research how living things can travel and survive in space
items.examples: Rocket take-off and re-entry, sustained living in space, International Space Station.

items.text: Examine the development of our knowledge through discoveries and technologies, and how these benefit humankind
items.examples: Compass, concrete, lenses, satellites, wheel.

items.text: Describe how Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples' Knowledges of the positions of the Sun, Moon and stars are used for navigation and wayfinding
